analysis.one_liner: Lets employers pay the lower tipped minimum wage for non-tipped work like cleaning and prep.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current Department of Labor rules, an employer who takes a tip credit must pay the full federal minimum wage ($7.25) when a tipped worker spends time on tasks that aren't tip-related, like cleaning, dishwashing, or prep work. This bill would change the legal definition of a tipped employee so that employers could pay the much lower tipped minimum wage ($2.13 in cash) for all of a worker's tasks — tipped or not — as long as the worker's tips and cash wages combined average out to at least $7.25. It would also let the employer choose the averaging period: a day, a week, every other week, or even a full month.
analysis.who_benefits: Restaurant and bar owners, and other employers of tipped workers, would save on labor costs. They could pay $2.13 in cash wages for hours their employees spend on non-tipped side work, shifting more of the burden of reaching the minimum wage onto customers' tips. Employers would also gain flexibility in choosing how long an averaging period to use — a month-long period can hide individual days when a worker's combined pay fell below the minimum.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the definition of a tipped employee so it does not depend on the employee's actual duties — an employer could pay the tipped minimum wage for tasks unrelated to tipped work as long as combined tips and direct wages reach the $7.25 federal minimum.
Current Department of Labor rules prohibit paying the tipped minimum wage for tasks that are not related to tipped work; the bill would override that rule.
The bill lets the employer choose the averaging period — as short as one day or as long as one month — over which tips and cash wages must total the federal minimum.
The bill's sponsor, Sen. Mike Braun (R-IN), introduced it on December 13, 2022, in the final weeks of the 117th Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Tipped workers themselves. Under the bill, their tips — which come from customers — would effectively subsidize hours spent on non-tipped side work, letting employers pay as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages for that time. Tips are unpredictable and customer-funded, so a worker's guaranteed cash income from the employer would shrink. A month-long averaging period could also mask stretches of several days when a worker's actual combined earnings fell below $7.25.

drawbacks.text: The bill would let employers pay as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages for non-tipped tasks, shifting more of the cost of those hours onto customers' tips and making workers' income more dependent on unpredictable tipping.

Because the employer picks the averaging period — up to a full month — the combined $7.25 floor would be measured over long stretches, which can hide individual days when a worker earned below minimum wage.

The bill carries no protections for workers in slow periods; if tips are low, the employer, not the customer, would still be on the hook only for $2.13 an hour plus whatever shortfall exists at the end of the averaging period.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows almost entirely to restaurant and bar owners through lower payroll costs, while the cost falls on tipped workers, whose take-home pay would rely more heavily on customer tips and whose guaranteed cash wages for side work would drop from $7.25 to $2.13 an hour. The averaging-period provision would make the protection weaker in practice than it sounds, since a worker could fall below the minimum wage on individual days without triggering employer back pay.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last three weeks of the 117th Congress, referred to the Senate labor committee the same day, and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun (R-IN) introduced the bill on December 13, 2022, three weeks before the 117th Congress ended.
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction, and the committee took no further action on it.
No vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tipped workers keep the existing Department of Labor rule requiring full minimum wage for non-tipped tasks, while restaurant owners did not obtain the lower payroll costs this bill would have allowed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there was no record to show how support or opposition split by party; it was carried by a single Republican senator.

industries.note: The bill would cut these employers' payroll costs by letting them pay $2.13 an hour in cash wages for non-tipped side work instead of $7.25, with customers' tips making up the difference. The savings to owners come directly out of what tipped workers are guaranteed from their employer.

Workers' guaranteed cash wages for side work would drop, and more of their income would depend on unpredictable tips. The employer-chosen averaging period could hide days when earnings fell below the minimum wage.
